In mathematics, a '''semiorthogonal decomposition''' is a way to divide a [[triangulated category]] into simpler pieces. One way to produce a semiorthogonal decomposition is from an '''exceptional collection''', a special sequence of objects in a triangulated category. For an [[algebraic variety]] ''X'', it has been fruitful to study semiorthogonal decompositions of the bounded [[derived category]] of [[coherent sheaves]], <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math>.

==Semiorthogonal decomposition==
Alexei Bondal and [[Mikhail Kapranov]] (1989) defined a '''semiorthogonal decomposition''' of a triangulated category <math>\mathcal{T}</math> to be a sequence <math>\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n</math> of [[strictly full subcategory|strictly full]] triangulated subcategories such that:{{sfn|Huybrechts|2006|loc=Definition 1.59}}
*for all <math>1\leq i<j\leq n</math> and all objects <math>A_i\in\mathcal{A}_i</math> and <math>A_j\in\mathcal{A}_j</math>, every morphism from <math>A_j</math> to <math>A_i</math> is zero. That is, there are "no morphisms from right to left".
*<math>\mathcal{T}</math> is generated by <math>\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n</math>. That is, the smallest strictly full triangulated subcategory of <math>\mathcal{T}</math> containing <math>\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n</math> is equal to <math>\mathcal{T}</math>.
The notation <math>\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n\rangle</math> is used for a semiorthogonal decomposition.

Having a semiorthogonal decomposition implies that every object of <math>\mathcal{T}</math> has a canonical "filtration" whose graded pieces are (successively) in the subcategories <math>\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n</math>. That is, for each object ''T'' of <math>\mathcal{T}</math>, there is a sequence
:<math>0=T_n\to T_{n-1}\to\cdots\to T_0=T</math>
of morphisms in <math>\mathcal{T}</math> such that the [[triangulated category#Definition|cone]] of <math>T_i\to T_{i-1}</math> is in <math>\mathcal{A}_i</math>, for each ''i''. Moreover, this sequence is unique up to a unique isomorphism.{{sfn|Bondal|Kapranov|1990|loc=Proposition 1.5}}

One can also consider "orthogonal" decompositions of a triangulated category, by requiring that there are no morphisms from <math>\mathcal{A}_i</math> to <math>\mathcal{A}_j</math> for any <math>i\neq j</math>. However, that property is too strong for most purposes. For example, for an (irreducible) [[smooth scheme|smooth]] [[projective variety]] ''X'' over a [[field (mathematics)|field]], the bounded [[derived category]] <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> of [[coherent sheaves]] never has a nontrivial orthogonal decomposition, whereas it may have a semiorthogonal decomposition, by the examples below.

A semiorthogonal decomposition of a triangulated category may be considered as analogous to a finite [[filtration (mathematics)|filtration]] of an [[abelian group]]. Alternatively, one may consider a semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rangle</math> as closer to a [[split exact sequence]], because the exact sequence <math>0\to\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{A}\to 0</math> of triangulated categories is split by the subcategory <math>\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{T}</math>, mapping isomorphically to <math>\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{A}</math>.

Using that observation, a semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{A}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{A}_n\rangle</math> implies a [[direct sum]] splitting of [[Grothendieck group]]s:
:<math>K_0(\mathcal{T})\cong K_0(\mathcal{A}_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus K_0(\mathcal{A_n}).</math>
For example, when <math>\mathcal{T}=\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> is the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a smooth projective variety ''X'', <math>K_0(\mathcal{T})</math> can be identified with the Grothendieck group <math>K_0(X)</math> of [[algebraic vector bundle]]s on ''X''. In this geometric situation, using that <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> comes from a [[dg-category]], a semiorthogonal decomposition actually gives a splitting of all the [[algebraic K-group]]s of ''X'':
:<math>K_i(X)\cong K_i(\mathcal{A}_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus K_i(\mathcal{A_n})</math>
for all ''i''.{{sfn|Orlov|2016|loc=Section 1.2}}

==Admissible subcategory==
One way to produce a semiorthogonal decomposition is from an admissible subcategory. By definition, a full triangulated subcategory <math>\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{T}</math> is '''left admissible''' if the inclusion functor <math>i\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{T}</math> has a left [[adjoint functor]], written <math>i^*</math>. Likewise, <math>\mathcal{A}\subset\mathcal{T}</math> is '''right admissible''' if the inclusion has a right adjoint, written <math>i^!</math>, and it is '''admissible''' if it is both left and right admissible.

A right admissible subcategory <math>\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{T}</math> determines a semiorthogonal decomposition
:<math>\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{B}^{\perp},\mathcal{B}\rangle</math>,
where
:<math>\mathcal{B}^{\perp}:=\{T\in\mathcal{T}: \operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{B},T)=0\}</math>
is the '''right orthogonal''' of <math>\mathcal{B}</math> in <math>\mathcal{T}</math>.{{sfn|Bondal|Kapranov|1990|loc=Proposition 1.5}} Conversely, every semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\mathcal{T}=\langle \mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rangle</math> arises in this way, in the sense that <math>\mathcal{B}</math> is right admissible and <math>\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{B}^{\perp}</math>. Likewise, for any semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\mathcal{T}=\langle \mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rangle</math>, the subcategory <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is left admissible, and <math>\mathcal{B}={}^{\perp}\mathcal{A}</math>, where
:<math>{}^{\perp}\mathcal{A}:=\{T\in\mathcal{T}: \operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathcal{A})=0\}</math>
is the '''left orthogonal''' of <math>\mathcal{A}</math>.

If <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is the bounded derived category of a smooth projective variety over a field ''k'', then every left or right admissible subcategory of <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is in fact admissible.{{sfn|Kuznetsov|2007|loc=Lemmas 2.10, 2.11, and 2.12}} By results of Bondal and [[Michel Van den Bergh]], this holds more generally for <math>\mathcal{T}</math> any regular proper triangulated category that is [[pseudo-abelian category|idempotent-complete]].{{sfn|Orlov|2016|loc=Theorem 3.16}}

Moreover, for a regular proper idempotent-complete triangulated category <math>\mathcal{T}</math>, a full triangulated subcategory is admissible [[if and only if]] it is regular and idempotent-complete. These properties are intrinsic to the subcategory.{{sfn|Orlov|2016|loc=Propositions 3.17 and 3.20}} For example, for ''X'' a smooth projective variety and ''Y'' a subvariety not equal to ''X'', the subcategory of <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> of objects supported on ''Y'' is not admissible.

==Exceptional collection==
Let ''k'' be a field, and let <math>\mathcal{T}</math> be a ''k''-linear triangulated category. An object ''E'' of <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is called '''exceptional''' if Hom(''E'',''E'') = ''k'' and Hom(''E'',''E''[''t'']) = 0 for all nonzero integers ''t'', where [''t''] is the [[triangulated category#Definition|shift functor]] in <math>\mathcal{T}</math>. (In the derived category of a smooth [[complex number|complex]] projective variety ''X'', the first-order [[deformation theory|deformation space]] of an object ''E'' is <math>\operatorname{Ext}^1_X(E,E)\cong \operatorname{Hom}(E,E[1])</math>, and so an [[exceptional object]] is in particular rigid. It follows, for example, that there are at most [[countably]] many exceptional objects in <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math>, up to isomorphism. That helps to explain the name.)

The triangulated subcategory generated by an exceptional object ''E'' is equivalent to the derived category <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(k)</math> of finite-dimensional ''k''-vector spaces, the simplest triangulated category in this context. (For example, every object of that subcategory is isomorphic to a finite direct sum of shifts of ''E''.)

Alexei Gorodentsev and Alexei Rudakov (1987) defined an '''exceptional collection''' to be a sequence of exceptional objects <math>E_1,\ldots,E_m</math> such that <math>\operatorname{Hom}(E_j,E_i[t])=0</math> for all ''i'' < ''j'' and all integers ''t''. (That is, there are "no morphisms from right to left".) In a proper triangulated category <math>\mathcal{T}</math> over ''k'', such as the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a smooth projective variety, every exceptional collection generates an admissible subcategory, and so it determines a semiorthogonal decomposition:
:<math>\mathcal{T}=\langle\mathcal{A},E_1,\ldots,E_m\rangle,</math>
where <math>\mathcal{A}=\langle E_1,\ldots,E_m\rangle^{\perp}</math>, and <math>E_i</math> denotes the full triangulated subcategory generated by the object <math>E_i</math>.{{sfn|Huybrechts|2006|loc=Lemma 1.58}} An exceptional collection is called '''full''' if the subcategory <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is zero. (Thus a full exceptional collection breaks the whole triangulated category up into finitely many copies of <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(k)</math>.)

In particular, if ''X'' is a smooth projective variety such that <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> has a full exceptional collection <math>E_1,\ldots,E_m</math>, then the [[algebraic K-theory|Grothendieck group]] of algebraic vector bundles on ''X'' is the [[free abelian group]] on the classes of these objects:
:<math>K_0(X)\cong \Z\{E_1,\ldots,E_m\}.</math>

A smooth complex projective variety ''X'' with a full exceptional collection must have trivial [[Hodge theory]], in the sense that <math>h^{p,q}(X)=0</math> for all <math>p\neq q</math>; moreover, the [[cycle class map]] <math>CH^*(X)\otimes\Q\to H^*(X,\Q)</math> must be an isomorphism.{{sfn|Marcolli|Tabuada|2015|loc=Proposition 1.9}}

==Examples==
The original example of a full exceptional collection was discovered by [[Alexander Beilinson]] (1978): the derived category of [[projective space]] over a field has the full exceptional collection
:<math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(\mathbf{P}^n)=\langle O,O(1),\ldots,O(n)\rangle</math>,
where O(''j'') for integers ''j'' are the [[coherent sheaf#Examples of vector bundles|line bundles on projective space]].{{sfn|Huybrechts|2006|loc=Corollary 8.29}} Full exceptional collections have also been constructed on all smooth projective [[toric varieties]], [[del Pezzo surface]]s, many [[projective homogeneous varieties]], and some other [[Fano varieties]].{{sfn|Kuznetsov|2014|loc=Section 2.2}}

More generally, if ''X'' is a smooth projective variety of positive dimension such that the [[coherent sheaf cohomology]] groups <math>H^i(X,O_X)</math> are zero for ''i'' > 0, then the object <math>O_X</math> in <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)</math> is exceptional, and so it induces a nontrivial semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)=\langle (O_X)^{\perp},O_X\rangle</math>. This applies to every [[Fano variety]] over a field of [[characteristic zero]], for example. It also applies to some other varieties, such as [[Enriques surface]]s and some surfaces of [[general type]].

A source of examples is Orlov's blowup formula concerning the [[blowing up|blowup]] <math>X = \operatorname{Bl}_Z(Y)</math> of a smooth projective variety <math>Y</math> at a smooth subvariety <math>Z</math> of codimension <math>k</math> with exceptional locus <math>\iota: E \simeq \mathbb{P}_Z(N_{Z/Y})\to X</math>. There is a semiorthogonal decomposition <math>D^b(X) = \langle \Phi_{1-k}(D^b(Z)), \ldots, \Phi_{-1}(D^b(Z)), \pi^*(D^b(Y))\rangle</math> where <math>\Phi_i:D^b(Z) \to D^b(X)</math> is the functor <math>\Phi_i(-) = \iota_*(\mathcal{O}_E(i)\otimes p^*(-))</math> where <math>p : X \to Y</math> is the natural projection map.<ref>{{Citation |last=Orlov |first=D O |date=1993-02-28 |title=Projective Bundles, Monoidal Transformations, and Derived Categories of Coherent Sheaves |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1070/im1993v041n01abeh002182 |journal=Russian Academy of Sciences. Izvestiya Mathematics |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=133–141 |doi=10.1070/im1993v041n01abeh002182 |bibcode=1993IzMat..41..133O |issn=1064-5632|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While these examples encompass a large number of well-studied derived categories, many naturally occurring triangulated categories are "indecomposable". In particular, for a smooth projective variety ''X'' whose [[canonical bundle]] <math>K_X</math> is [[basepoint-free]], every semiorthogonal decomposition <math>\text{D}^{\text{b}}(X)=\langle\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\rangle</math> is trivial in the sense that <math>\mathcal{A}</math> or <math>\mathcal{B}</math> must be zero.{{sfn|Kuznetsov|2014|loc=Section 2.5}} For example, this applies to every variety which is [[Calabi–Yau]] in the sense that its canonical bundle is trivial.
